'Your cross is silver,' she said. Her voice was dry, like leaves skittering on pavement. 'But I was not killed by a cross. I was killed by hunger. I was killed by loneliness. I was killed by a village that decided I was dangerous because I did not marry and because my garden grew when theirs did not. What does your silver do against that?'

Andrej found he had no answer. The ritual words caught in his throat, not from fear but from the sudden understanding that the exorcism assumed a kind of evil he was not witnessing.

The Striga looked at him for a long time. 'Go back,' she said. 'Tell them I am here. Not because I want to be, but because they made me and forgot to unmake me.'

She rose back to her ledge and disappeared among the rocks. Andrej walked back down the pass without stopping and found the old man still on his stone.

'You saw her,' the old man said. 'And did your cross drive her away?'

'No.'

'She was a girl once. The Striga is not born. She is made.'

Andrej never walked the pass alone again. He did not speak of the Striga from his pulpit, but he changed the way he listened to his parishioners. When they spoke of cursed women and haunted places, he asked not what evil had possessed them, but what cruelty had been done to them first.

Travelers still hear weeping in the pass through the High Tatras. In Stara Lubovna, some leave small offerings at the trailhead — bread, salt, a candle. Not to appease a monster. To remember a girl.
themes: the making of monsters by human cruelty
the failure of exorcism against injustice
moral: A curse born of human cruelty cannot be lifted by divine ritual alone; it demands that the living acknowledge the wrong that created it.
source: Slovak oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: The Polkan at the Ridge
summary: A shepherd boy encounters the Polkan shapeshifter on a mountain ridge and survives by offering it neither fear nor aggression, but a riddle it cannot answer without revealing its true form.
full_text:
Tomas was twelve years old and already trusted with the village flock, which meant he spent his days on the high ridges above Orava where the grass grew short and sweet and the wind carried the smell of pine resin and distant rain. He knew every stone, every gully, every place where a wolf might shelter. What he did not know was the Polkan.

His grandfather had warned him, as all the old men of Orava warned the young shepherds. 'If you see a figure on the ridge that is too tall, too still, or moving in a way that does not match its legs, do not approach it. The Polkan shows itself as a man, a bear, a shadow, or smoke, and it is none of these things. It is the ridge itself, given hunger.'

Tomas had forgotten the warning, as boys do, until the evening he saw it.

The sun was low and the flock was gathering for the slow walk back to the village pen. Tomas counted the sheep — thirty-one, all present — and then he looked up and saw a figure standing on the ridge. It was shaped like a man but too large, perhaps seven feet tall, and its proportions were wrong. The shoulders were too wide. The arms hung too low. And the head seemed to rotate a fraction too far when it turned to look at him.

The sheep went silent. The wind stopped.

Then the figure changed. It was not sudden but a slow, sickening flow, like wax melting and reforming. The man-shape compressed and bulged and became something with a hump and a snout, a bear-shaped thing that was still not a bear because its eyes remained exactly where the man's eyes had been.

Tomas did not run. He sat down on the grass, set his staff across his knees, and spoke. 'I have a riddle. If you cannot answer it, you must leave me and my flock in peace. That is the old bargain.'

The Polkan tilted its massive head. The air around it seemed to lean forward.

Tomas said, 'What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening?'

This was not his riddle. It was ancient, older than the village, older than the mountains, from a land far to the south where men built temples of white stone. Tomas did not know if it was true. He only knew that his grandfather had told him the Polkan, like all old things, could be bound by old words.

The creature sat down on the ridge like a dog. Its shape flickered — man, bear, smoke, man again. It could not answer. Not because the riddle was too hard, but because the answer was a man, and the Polkan had never been a man. It could copy the shape but not the history.

After a long silence the creature stood, flickered once more, and was simply gone, as though the ridge had swallowed it. The wind returned. The sheep bleated.

Tomas walked the flock home in the dark. His grandfather listened and nodded. 'You gave it a human answer to a human riddle. The Polkan can mimic a man's shape but not a man's story. Remember that, boy. It is the only weapon you need.'

The Polkan still walks the ridge above Orava. But the riddle is remembered, and as long as it is remembered, the shepherds are safe.
themes: the power of riddles and ancient bargains
the boundary between nature and spirit
moral: The creatures of the wild can mimic human form but never human experience, and it is the lived story of a mortal life that no ancient spirit can replicate.
source: Slovak oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: The Vodnik of the Mountain Stream
summary: A fisherman who has grown too greedy learns a lesson from the Vodnik, the water spirit who guards the mountain streams and punishes those who take more than they need.
full_text:
Martin was the finest fisherman on the Hron river and he knew it. His nets were always full, his baskets always heavy, and his wife Alzbeta always had silver coins to show at market day. But the thing about silver is that it is never enough. Each season his nets grew wider and his ambitions greedier, and the river gave what he asked because it had always given and he had never thought to ask why.

The old fishermen spoke of the Vodnik — the water spirit who lived in the deep pools beneath the willows and the old stone bridge. They said he was a small, pale man with green hair and eyes like pond water, and that he collected the souls of the drowned in porcelain cups. They said he could be bargained with but never cheated. Martin had laughed at these stories.

'The river gives fish. I take fish. That is the arrangement,' he said.

'The arrangement,' said old Jozef the net-mender, 'is that you take what you need and leave the rest. Push too hard and he will change the terms.'

Martin pushed harder. He fished at night during the spawning runs. He cast in the shallows where the young gathered. The silver flowed in, and the river grew quieter each year. Fewer trout leaped at dawn.

One evening in late summer he cast his net at the deepest pool beneath the stone bridge. When he pulled it up it was heavier than any catch before. He hauled it to the bank and found not a fish but a porcelain cup, old and cracked, with a faded blue pattern of fish swimming in a circle.

Then the voice came from the river itself. 'You know what that is.'

Every fisherman along the Hron knew the stories. The Vodnik kept the souls of the drowned in cups like this.

'I did not ask for this,' Martin said.

'You did not ask because you never ask. You only take. You take the young fish and the spawning runs, as though the river had no bottom. But there is a bottom, Martin. I am the bottom.'

'What do you want?'

'Enough. Leave enough for the river to live. Leave enough so that when your arms cannot cast a net, there will still be fish for the boys who come after you.'

Martin set the cup down on the grass. 'I will change.'

'Words are water. I will be watching.'

Martin fished only in the proper seasons after that. He used narrower nets and threw back the spawning females. The first year was hard. The silver diminished. But the second year the river recovered — trout returned to the shallows, crayfish multiplied beneath the stones — and his catches, though less frequent, were finer than ever.

On a summer evening five years later Martin sat at the deep pool. He was old now, his hands gnarled. His sons fished the Hron, and his grandsons would too. He set a porcelain cup at the water's edge — an offering, a thank-you, a remembrance.

The water rippled once, as though something beneath had smiled. Martin smiled back.

'Enough,' he said to the river, and the word was not a limit but a prayer.
themes: the Vodnik as judge and keeper
moral: The river gives abundantly to those who take only what they need, but punishes the greedy until they learn the meaning of enough.
source: Slovak oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: The Psoglav of the Unmarked Graves
summary: A monstrous hound with a human face and a single eye in its forehead feeds on the forgotten dead buried without crosses, and those who hear its digging at night know which graves the village tried to erase.
full_text:
In the hills above Jajce, where the forests grow thick and the paths split without warning, there are graves that bear no name. No wooden cross marks them. No stone stands over them. The earth is smooth and undisturbed, as though nothing lies beneath.

But something knows.

The Psoglav walks the crossroads at night. It has the body of a hound — lean, dark-furred, built for running through the underbrush without a sound. Its legs are long. Its paws are wide and sharp-clawed. Its tail hangs low, almost brushing the ground. But its face is human. A human nose. Human lips pulled back over teeth too large for any human mouth. And in the center of its forehead, above the bridge of the nose, a single eye. Not a human eye. An eye that sees through stone, through earth, through the layers of soil and root and bone.

The Psoglav sees the dead that the village buried in shame.

It was old Manojlo who first spoke of it, back when the mill still ground flour and the church bell still rang at dusk. 'There is a thing in the crossroads,' he said. 'It digs at night. It feeds on the ones we did not bury properly.' The villagers looked at one another. They knew which graves bore no cross.

The young wife of the blacksmith was the first to hear it. She lay awake one autumn night, her husband away in Travnik, and from the crossroads below the hill came the sound of claws on earth. Not the scrape of a fox or the digging of a badger. Something heavier. Something deliberate. She did not go to the window. She pulled the blanket over her head and waited for dawn.

In the morning, the earth at the crossroads was torn open. A shallow grave, unmarked, uncovered. The body within was not whole.

The priest was called. He blessed the ground. He drove a cross into the earth. But the cross was pulled out by morning, lying on its side in the grass like a discarded tool.

The old people were not surprised. 'The Psoglav does not respect crosses,' they said. 'It feeds on the dead that the living refused to honor. If the village buries a man without a name, the Psoglav will find him. If the village buries a woman without a prayer, the Psoglav will dig her up. The cross is nothing to the Psoglav. The cross is for the living, not for the dead.'

The blacksmith's wife asked what could be done. The old people shook their heads. 'Name the dead,' they said. 'Pray for them. Mark their graves. The Psoglav feeds on forgetting. Give the dead their names, and the Psoglav has nothing to eat.'

The village remembered. Slowly, reluctantly, they went to the crossroads and the unmarked places. They spoke the names of the dead. They drove new crosses into the earth. They prayed the prayers they had neglected.

The digging stopped. The Psoglav walked on.

But the old people warned: the Psoglav does not leave Bosnia. It walks the crossroads of every village, every valley, every mountain path. It sees every grave. It knows every name. And if the living forget the dead — if the crosses rot and the names fade — the Psoglav will return.

It always returns.
moral: The dead that the living refuse to name are not forgotten. Something remembers them, and it is hungry.
source: Bosnian oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: The Drekavac in the Cemetery
summary: A wailing spirit that rises from the graves of unbaptized children cries through the villages of Bosnia at night, and those who listen too closely hear the names of the children no one spoke aloud.
full_text:
The Drekavac cries at the edge of the cemetery, where the old wall crumbles and the grass grows high over the graves that no one tends.

It is not a large sound. It is not the howl of a wolf or the shriek of an owl. It is smaller than that — thinner, higher, like a child calling from very far away, or a child calling from very close but through a door that will not open. The sound has a shape to it, the old women say. It rises and falls like breathing. It pauses like a question.

The Drekavac is the spirit of a child who died without baptism. In the villages of Bosnia, where the rivers run cold and the winters are long, not every child survived to the naming day. Some were born in the depth of winter, when the roads were impassable and the priest was three valleys away. Some were born sick, their breath shallow, their skin already blue. They died before the holy water touched their foreheads. They died without a name.

These children do not rest. They rise from the graves as the Drekavac — small, formless, made of sound and longing. They do not have teeth. They do not have claws. They have only their cry, and the cry is enough.

The Drekavac wanders the village at night. It passes the houses where mothers wept. It lingers at the doors of fathers who could not afford the burial. It cries at the cemetery wall, where the unbaptized graves lie in a row, marked only by stones that bear no inscription.

Old Mila heard it once, sixty years ago, when she was still a girl sleeping in the loft above the kitchen. The sound came through the shutters, thin and persistent, like a thread of ice pressed against her ear. She did not move. She did not speak. She lay very still and listened.

The Drekavac cried for a long time. Then it stopped, suddenly, as though it had been called. Mila heard footsteps — real footsteps, human — on the road below. A man was walking, his boots heavy on the frozen ground. The Drekavac did not cry again that night.

Mila told the story for sixty years. 'The Drekavac is not evil,' she always said. 'It is lonely. It cries because it has no name. It cries because no one speaks its name, because no one remembers it, because it was born into a world that would not hold it.'

The villagers learned to light candles at the cemetery wall on the night before All Souls. They poured water on the unmarked graves. They whispered the names of the children they had lost — names given in private, names spoken only to the wind, names that no priest had recorded.

The Drekavac still cries sometimes. In the villages above the Neretva, where the mountains rise sharp and the snow comes early, mothers still hear it through the shutters. But they do not fear it. They light a candle. They speak a name. They pour water on the earth.

The crying fades. The night grows quiet. The Drekavac returns to its grave, comforted for another year.
moral: Every child deserves a name, and those who are denied one in life will cry for it in death.
source: Bosnian oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: The Dzin of the Bazaar
summary: A spirit bound to the old marketplaces of Bosnia, the Dzin grants fortunes to those it favors and misfortune to those who deal dishonestly, serving as an unseen guardian of fair trade.
full_text:
In the old bazaar of Sarajevo, where the copper sellers hammer their trays and the coffee sellers grind their beans in the shadow of the mosque, there is a spirit that watches the scales.

The Dzin is not visible. It does not walk the cobblestones in the shape of a man or a beast. It is something else — something between the smoke of the coffee house and the heat of the coppersmith's forge, something that exists in the spaces where deals are made and promises are spoken.

The merchants of the bazaar have always known about the Dzin. They do not speak of it to outsiders. They do not write about it in their books. They know it the way they know the weight of a full sack of coffee or the smell of rain coming over the mountains — by instinct, by tradition, by the hard lessons of their grandfathers.

The Dzin favors the honest merchant. When a seller weights his scales fairly, when he gives full measure, when he does not cheat the customer or the craftsman — the Dzin whispers. It whispers into the ear as the merchant sleeps. It shows him the coming season. It shows him which goods will be needed. It shows him the path to profit, not through cunning but through the steady rhythm of honest work.

But the Dzin punishes the dishonest. When a seller adds water to his milk or sand to his grain, when he weighs his scales with lead on one side, when he lies about the origin of his goods — the Dzin acts. Not with violence. Not with fire or flood. With something worse. The dishonest merchant finds his goods rotting in the storeroom. His customers vanish. His partners withdraw their trust. His fortune unravels thread by thread, as though pulled by invisible hands.

Husein, who sold carpets near the Latin Bridge, once told the story of his uncle Mehmed. Mehmed had been a successful man, a man with a fine shop and a reputation for quality. But in a moment of weakness, he sold a carpet of mixed wool and cotton as pure wool to a buyer from Mostar. The profit was small. The consequence was not.

Within a year, Mehmed's shop lost half its customers. His best weavers left for other masters. A shipment of dyes arrived spoiled. His partner accused him of hidden debts. Everything Mehmed touched soured. Everything he built crumbled.

He went to the old men of the bazaar. They listened. They nodded. They told him about the Dzin.

Mehmed traveled to Mostar. He found the buyer. He returned the money. He admitted what he had done. He spoke the truth aloud, in the marketplace, where all could hear.

The Dzin did not forgive quickly. But it forgave. Within two seasons, Mehmed's shop recovered. His customers returned. His reputation, though scarred, healed. He never cheated again.

The merchants of Sarajevo still speak of the Dzin in the language of gesture and implication. They tap the scale twice before weighing. They pour the first cup of coffee to the ground. They look at their partner's eyes when a deal is struck, searching for the flicker of dishonesty that the Dzin sees instantly.

The Dzin is patient. It does not punish in haste. It watches. It waits. It remembers every transaction, every weight, every word spoken in the bazaar. And when the time comes — for reward or for ruin — it acts with the precision of a coppersmith's hammer.
moral: Honest work is rewarded and dishonest dealing is undone, though the reckoning may take its time.
source: Bosnian oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: The Vila of Maglić
summary: A winged mountain spirit dances on the summit of Maglić in storms, and the shepherd who follows her song into the clouds returns with impossible knowledge — or does not return at all.
full_text:
The peak of Maglić is the highest point in Bosnia, and the Vila lives there.

She is not always visible. Most days the mountain is just stone and snow, wind and silence. But when the storms come — when the black clouds pile up from the direction of the Adriatic and the thunder rolls across the valleys like drums — the Vila appears. She dances on the summit. Her feet touch the bare rock. Her hair flies behind her, long and white, whipped by winds that would throw a man to his knees. Her wings — if they are wings, or if they are just the storm itself wrapped around her body — spread wide, catching the lightning like a net catches fish.

The shepherds of the Sutjeska valley have always known about the Vila. They see her on storm days, a figure against the sky, white and terrible and beautiful. Some of them have heard her sing. The song is not in any human language. It is older than language. It is the sound of the mountain speaking to the sky.

Stojan was a shepherd from Tjentište who climbed Maglić once, in a summer storm, because he was young and because he was foolish and because he thought the Vila was a woman and not something else entirely. He climbed through the wind. He climbed through rain that hit his face like stones. He reached the summit.

The Vila was there. She was exactly as the old men described — white-haired, white-winged, her feet bare on the rock. She looked at Stojan with eyes that were the color of glacier ice, and she spoke.

She did not speak in words. She spoke in images. She showed Stojan the future of his village — the flood that would come in autumn, the fire that would take the church in winter, the child that would be born in spring with a birthmark shaped like a crescent moon. She showed him the path of his own life — the years of good grazing, the drought that would thin his flock, the woman he would marry, the sons who would carry his name.

Stojan listened. He did not speak. When the vision ended, the Vila was gone. The storm passed. Stojan climbed down from Maglić, his legs shaking, his mind full of things he could not yet understand.

He told the villagers what he had seen. Some believed him. Some did not. But when the flood came in autumn, and the fire took the church in winter, and the child was born with the crescent mark — they believed.

Stojan lived a long life. His flock grew large. He married the woman the Vila had shown him. His sons carried his name. But he never climbed Maglić again. 'The Vila shows you the truth,' he told his grandchildren, 'and the truth is a weight that the young shoulders cannot bear. She is kind in her way. She is honest. But her honesty is the honesty of the mountain — it does not care if you are ready to hear it.'

The shepherds still climb Maglić on storm days. Some hear the song. Some see the figure on the summit. A few have climbed high enough to speak with her. They come back changed — quieter, older in the eyes, carrying knowledge that sits heavy in their chests like a stone.

The Vila dances. The storm gathers. The mountain stands. And the shepherds decide, one by one, whether they are ready to climb.
moral: Truth is not a gift but a burden, and those who seek it must be prepared to carry its weight.
source: Bosnian oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: The Nav and the Weaver
summary: A jealous night demon descends on women who weave beautiful cloth, tangling their threads and spoiling their patterns, because the Nav cannot bear to see anything more perfect than itself.
full_text:
The Nav comes at night, and it hates beautiful things.

It is a demon — small, dark, with wings like a bat's and teeth like needles. It has no fixed shape. Sometimes it is the size of a cat. Sometimes it is the size of a fist. It moves through the walls of houses, through the cracks in the plaster, through the gaps between the stones. It finds its way to the room where the loom stands.

The Nav hates the loom. It hates the thread stretched tight across the frame. It hates the pattern taking shape under the weaver's hands — the red and gold, the white and blue, the designs that have been passed down from mother to daughter for a hundred generations. The Nav cannot weave. It cannot make beautiful things. It can only destroy.

In the village of Prozor, there lived a woman named Šehira who was the finest weaver in the valley. Her carpets were sold in Mostar and Sarajevo. Her patterns were known by name — the river pattern, the crescent pattern, the pattern of interlocking diamonds that her grandmother had invented and that no other weaver had successfully copied.

The Nav came to Šehira's house three times in one week. The first night, it tangled the red thread so thoroughly that Šehira spent the entire morning undoing the knots. The second night, it left a stain on the white wool that could not be washed out. The third night, it destroyed the carpet entirely — pulled every thread from the frame, snapped the warp, scattered the shuttles across the floor.

Šehira sat in the morning light and looked at the ruins of her work. She did not weep. She did not curse. She went to the old women of the village and asked what they knew of the Nav.

The old women knew. They told her the Nav feeds on jealousy. It cannot create. It can only undo. And it is drawn to beauty the way a moth is drawn to flame — irresistibly, destructively.

They told her the remedy. 'Hang a sprig of wormwood above the loom,' they said. 'Place a needle in the water at the foot of the frame. Speak the name of the Nav three times — not aloud, but in your mind, with the thread between your fingers. The Nav will not come again.'

Šehira did as she was told. She hung the wormwood. She placed the needle. She wove, and as she wove, she spoke the name of the Nav — silently, in the rhythm of the shuttle, in the counting of the threads.

The Nav did not come that night. Nor the next. Nor the next.

But the old women warned Šehira: the Nav is not destroyed by these things. It is only discouraged. It will move to another house, another village, another weaver. It will find someone whose beauty offends it. It will tangle their threads and stain their wool and destroy their work.

Šehira taught her remedies to every weaver in the valley. They hung wormwood. They placed needles. They spoke the name. The Nav wandered, but it found fewer victims.

The old women say that the Nav is still out there, somewhere in Bosnia, searching for beauty to destroy. It moves through the walls. It finds the loom. It reaches out its needle-teeth for the thread.

But the weavers are ready. They have been ready for generations.
moral: Beauty will always draw envy, but those who know the remedy can protect what they create.
source: Bosnian oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: Krsnik, the Slovene Daylight Hero
summary: A heroic spirit of Slovenian folklore, the Krsnik is a being of light who fights the dark forces of the Kurent, protecting villages from evil.
full_text:
In the folklore of Slovenia, there exists a being of pure light called the Krsnik. He is a hero born under a caul, a child destined from birth to fight the forces of darkness. The Krsnik can see spirits that ordinary humans cannot, and he has the power to transform into a white horse, a wolf, or an eagle. By night, his soul leaves his body and flies across the mountains to battle the Kurent, the dark spirits that bring disease and misfortune to the villages.

The Krsnik's greatest battle occurs every year, on a night when the boundary between worlds is thin. He meets the leader of the Kurent in the sky above Mount Triglav. Their battle lasts until dawn, lightning flashing from their weapons, thunder rolling from their voices. If the Krsnik wins, the village will have a year of plenty. If he falters, disease and hardship follow. The people never see this battle, but they feel it in the rumble of the earth and the crack of the storm.

An old story from the Julian Alps tells of a Krsnik who grew weary of his duty. He wanted to live a normal life, to marry and have children. But the Kurent grew stronger in his absence, and the village suffered. Finally, the Krsnik returned to his post. He fought the Kurent for three nights and three days, until both were exhausted. The Krsnik prevailed, but he was never the same. He became a lonely figure, living apart from the village, always watching the sky. The Slovenian people remember that the Krsnik sacrifices his own happiness for their safety, and they honor him with prayers and small offerings left at crossroads.
moral: True heroism is the willingness to sacrifice one's own happiness for others.
source: Slovenian oral tradition, Slavic folklore

title: Vodnik, the Slovenian Water Sprite
summary: A mischievous water sprite of Slovenian folklore, Vodnik lives in rivers and lakes, drowning the unwary but also helping those he favors.
full_text:
In the rivers and lakes of Slovenia, from the emerald waters of Lake Bled to the swift currents of the Sava River, there lives a water spirit called Vodnik. He appears as an old man with a green beard and hair, his skin tinted blue from the cold water. His eyes are like dark pools, deep and impossible to read. Vodnik rules his domain absolutely. He can calm the waters for the fisherman he likes or raise waves to capsize the boat of the one who offends him.

Vodnik is capricious. He drowns the careless and rewards the respectful. A child who throws stones at the water or yells at the river may feel an invisible hand pull at their ankle, a warning from Vodnik. A fisherman who offers a coin to the water before casting his line will find the fish biting. Vodnik also steals beautiful women, pulling them beneath the surface to be his brides in his underwater palace.

A tale from the town of Radovljica tells of a young woman named Maja who was taken by Vodnik. She was washing clothes by the river when a hand of green water pulled her under. The village mourned. Three years later, a man saw Maja sitting by the river at dawn. She was pale but alive. 'Vodnik released me,' she said. 'He said I was too sad to keep.' She returned to the village but was never quite the same. She could predict the weather and the movement of fish. She was touched by the water spirit, and the people treated her with a mixture of awe and caution. Vodnik continues to watch the waters of Slovenia, and the people continue to respect him, leaving small offerings at bridges and riverbanks to stay in his favor.
moral: Water gives and takes; respect its power.
source: Slovenian oral tradition, Slavic folklore
